paragraphs: You can easily imagine what kind of father such a man would be and how he would bring up his children. His behavior as a father was exactly what you would expect. He abandoned the child of his marriage with Adelaïda Ivanovna completely—not from malice, nor because of his marital grievances, but simply because he forgot him. While he was wearying everyone with his tears and complaints and turning his house into a sink of debauchery, a faithful servant of the family, Grigory, took the three-year-old Mitya into his care. If he hadn’t looked after him, there would have been no one even to change the baby’s little shirt.

It happened, moreover, that the child’s relations on his mother’s side forgot him too at first. His grandfather was no longer living. His widow, Mitya’s grandmother, had moved to Moscow and was seriously ill, and the daughters were married. So Mitya remained for almost a whole year in old Grigory’s charge and lived with him in the servant’s cottage. But even if his father had remembered him (he could not, in fact, have been altogether unaware of his existence), he would have sent him back to the cottage, as the child would only have been in the way of his debaucheries. Then a cousin of Mitya’s mother, Pyotr Alexandrovitch Miüsov, happened to return from Paris. He lived abroad for many years afterwards, but at that time he was quite a young man, and stood out among the Miüsovs as a man of enlightened ideas and European culture, who had been in the capitals and abroad. Towards the end of his life he became a Liberal of the type common in the forties and fifties. In the course of his career he had come into contact with many of the most Liberal men of his time, both in Russia and abroad. He had known Proudhon and Bakunin personally, and in his declining years he was very fond of describing the three days of the Paris Revolution of February 1848, hinting that he himself had almost taken part in the fighting on the barricades. This was one of the happiest memories of his youth. He had an independent property of about a thousand souls, counting in the old style. His splendid estate lay on the outskirts of our little town and bordered on the lands of our famous monastery. Almost as soon as he came into the estate, Pyotr Alexandrovitch began an endless lawsuit with the monastery over the rights of fishing in the river or wood-cutting in the forest—I don’t know exactly which. He regarded it as his duty as a citizen and a man of culture to open an attack on the “clericals.” He heard all about Adelaïda Ivanovna, whom he of course remembered and in whom he had at one time been interested. When he learned of Mitya’s existence, he stepped in, in spite of all his youthful indignation and contempt for Fyodor Pavlovitch. He met Fyodor Pavlovitch for the first time and told him straight out that he wished to take charge of the child’s education. Long afterwards he used to tell, as a characteristic touch, that when he began to speak of Mitya, Fyodor Pavlovitch looked for some time as though he did not understand what child he was talking about, and even as though he was surprised to hear that he had a little son in the house. The story may have been exaggerated, yet it must have been something like the truth.

Fyodor Pavlovitch was fond of acting all his life, of suddenly playing an unexpected part, sometimes with no motive at all and even to his own plain disadvantage, as in this case. This habit, however, is characteristic of a great many people, some of them very clever, unlike Fyodor Pavlovitch. Pyotr Alexandrovitch carried the business through vigorously. He was appointed, together with Fyodor Pavlovitch, joint guardian of the child, who had a small property, a house and land, left him by his mother. Mitya did in fact pass into this cousin’s keeping. But the cousin had no family of his own, and once he had secured the revenues of his estates he was in a hurry to return to Paris. So he left the boy in the charge of one of his cousins, a lady living in Moscow. It came about that, once he had settled permanently in Paris, he too forgot the child, especially when the February Revolution broke out and made an impression on his mind that he remembered all the rest of his life. The Moscow lady died, and Mitya passed into the care of one of her married daughters. I believe he changed his home a fourth time later on. I won’t go into that now, as I shall have much to tell later about Fyodor Pavlovitch’s firstborn, and must confine myself now to the most essential facts about him, without which I could not begin my story.

In the first place, this Mitya, or rather Dmitri Fyodorovitch, was the only one of Fyodor Pavlovitch’s three sons who grew up believing that he had property and that he would be independent when he came of age. He had an irregular boyhood and youth. He did not finish his studies at the gymnasium. He got into a military school, then went to the Caucasus, was promoted, fought a duel and was demoted to the ranks, earned promotion again, led a wild life and spent a good deal of money. He did not begin to receive any income from Fyodor Pavlovitch until he came of age, and until then he ran into debt. He saw and met his father for the first time on coming of age, when he visited our neighborhood on purpose to settle with him about his property. He seems not to have liked his father. He did not stay long with him and made haste to get away. He had managed only to get a sum of money and to enter into an agreement for future payments from the estate. Of its revenues and its value he was unable (a fact worth noting) to get any statement from his father on this occasion. Fyodor Pavlovitch noticed for the first time then (this, too, should be noted) that Mitya had a vague and exaggerated idea of his property. Fyodor Pavlovitch was very well satisfied with this, as it fitted his own designs. He gathered only that the young man was frivolous, unruly, violent in his passions, impatient and dissipated, and that if he could only get ready money he would be satisfied, though only, of course, for a short time. So Fyodor Pavlovitch began to take advantage of this, sending him small doles from time to time, installments. In the end, four years later, Mitya lost patience and came a second time to our little town to settle up once and for all with his father. To his amazement it turned out that he had nothing; that it was difficult even to get an account; that he had received the whole value of his property in sums of money from Fyodor Pavlovitch and was perhaps even in debt to him; that under various agreements he had entered into of his own wish at various earlier dates, he had no right to expect anything more; and so on, and so on. The young man was overwhelmed. He suspected deceit and cheating and was almost beside himself. And indeed this circumstance led to the catastrophe, the account of which forms the subject of my first introductory story, or rather the outward side of it. But before I pass to that story I must say a little about Fyodor Pavlovitch’s other two sons, and where they came from.
